papers.title: Roman Hitting Functions
papers.abstract: Roman domination is one of few examples where the related extension problem is polynomial-time solvable even if the original decision problem is NP-complete. This is interesting as it allows to establish polynomial-delay enumeration algorithms for listing minimal Roman dominating functions, while it is open for more than four decades if all minimal dominating sets of a graph can be enumerated with polynomial delay, or even in output-polynomial time. To find the reason why this is the case, we combine the idea of hitting set with the idea of Roman domination. We hence obtain and study a new problem, called Roman Hitting Function, generalizing Roman Domination towards hypergraphs. This allows us to delineate the frontier of polynomial-delay enumerability. Our main focus is on the extension version of this problem, as this was the key problem when coping with Roman domination functions. While doing this, we find some conditions under which the Extension Roman Hitting Function problem is NP-complete. We then use parameterized complexity as a tool to get a better understanding of why Extension Roman Hitting Function behaves in this way. We discuss another generalization of Extension Roman Domination, where both a lower and an upper bound on the sought minimal Roman domination function is provided. The additional upper bound makes the problem hard, and the applied parameterized complexity analysis provides hardness results. From the viewpoint of Parameterized Complexity, the studies on extension problems are quite interesting as they provide more and more examples of parameterized problems complete for W[3], a complexity class with only very few natural members known some years ago. We employ our findings to present polynomial-delay and FPT-delay enumeration algorithms for Roman hitting functions, also drawing the borderline between polynomial delay and transversal hardness.

papers.title: Concave Run Budgets and Restart Width
papers.abstract: A source-to-target path in an edge-labelled DAG uses each label in some number of maximal runs, with a label used in \(r\) runs charged according to a nondecreasing concave rational tariff \(f(r)\). We seek a path of total charge at most \(B\), or a shortest such path. We parameterize by restart width \(\wr\), the maximum number of labels that have already appeared and can still begin a new run at some vertex. It is at most live width but can be arbitrarily smaller. Let \(J_f(T)\) denote the number of distinct marginal rates of \(f\) up to horizon \(T\). A lazy-commitment dynamic program solves minimum charge and feasibility in \(J_f(T)^{\wr}\poly(N)\) time, allowing arbitrary per-label tariffs and unbounded charge magnitudes. Thus the problem is FPT whenever \(J_f\) is effectively subpolynomial. Conversely, for every fixed tariff with \(J_f(T)\ge T^\delta\) eventually, feasibility is NP-complete and W[1]-hard in \(\wr\), even on planar bipartite DAGs of maximum degree three and treewidth two whose paths have equal length, and admits no \(g(\wr)N^{o(\wr)}\) algorithm under ETH. The reduction uses positive pairwise Jensen-gap charges, requires no denominator assumption, and covers harmonic, geometric, and power-law tariffs. A \(k\)-colour clique instance has width at most \(2k+1\), improved to \(k+1\) for polynomially bounded denominators. We further exhibit arbitrarily close tariffs with opposite parameterized complexity, give an FPT budget-relaxing scheme and accuracy obstruction, establish few-label hardness and W[P]-membership, and identify separate hardness from binary-encoded lengths. Oscillating plan growth and non-effective subpolynomial bounds remain open.

papers.title: Algorithms and Complexity of Connectivity Switching in Graphs
papers.abstract: We study computational problems in switch graphs. A switch graph consists of a vertex set and a set of switches, which are collections of edge sets. The goal is to find a configuration, that is, a selection of one edge set per switch, such that the resulting graph satisfies a desired property. This general framework unifies several switching models from prior work, with applications in solving Boolean equation systems, network routing, and SNP genotyping. We focus on connectivity-related switching problems, such as finding a configuration that yields a connected graph (global connectivity) or that connects a specific pair of vertices (local connectivity), presenting polynomial-time algorithms and establishing NP-completeness results depending on the switch structure. For local connectivity, we obtain a full complexity dichotomy. Furthermore, we introduce a natural weighted variant and analyze its parameterized complexity, proving W[1]-hardness with respect to the solution weight via reductions from restricted variants of the weighted satisfiability problem (WSAT). As a byproduct, we resolve an open question of Kanj and Szeider (TCS 2015) on the parameterized complexity of a specific WSAT variant.

papers.title: Linear-Time Optimal Leaf Roots beyond 3-Leaf Powers
papers.abstract: A $k$-leaf power for an integer $k \geq 2$ is a graph $G$ that permits a $k$-leaf root, a tree $T$ with leaf set $V(G)$ such that, for all distinct vertices $x,y \in V(G)$, their distance in $T$ is at most $k$ if and only if $xy$ is an edge of $G$. Constructing such trees is motivated by the reconstruction of phylogenetic trees from similarity data. For every fixed $k$, Lafond [ACM Trans. Algorithms 2023] showed that $k$-leaf powers can be recognized in polynomial time. Recently, Dupr\'e la Tour, Lafond, and Ndiaye [SODA 2026] proved that the problem becomes NP-complete when $k$ is part of the input and that deciding whether a graph is a $k$-leaf power for some $k$ is NP-complete as well. Le and Rosenke [J. Graph Algorithms Appl. 2024] proposed a different algorithmic perspective by studying \emph{optimal leaf roots} of graphs $G$, that is, the $k$-leaf roots of $G$ with minimum possible $k$. This smallest $k$-value is called the \emph{leaf rank} of $G$. They showed that optimal leaf roots of chordal cographs, a class of unbounded leaf rank, can be constructed in linear time. However, chordal cographs do not even contain all $3$-leaf powers. This paper extends linear-time optimal-leaf-root construction to three natural superclasses of the $3$-leaf powers, the $(\text{bull},\text{gem})$-free, the $(\text{bull},\text{dart})$-free, and the $(\text{dart},\text{gem})$-free chordal graphs. Except for the latter case, which follows from known results, our methods are based on structural decompositions of bull-free chordal graphs. In particular, the relevant $(\text{bull},\text{gem})$-free graphs decompose into chordal cographs attached to a tree, while the $(\text{bull},\text{dart})$-free case reduces to trees and powers of paths.

papers.title: A short proof of Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture
papers.abstract: We give a short alternative proof of Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture, recently proved by OpenAI. Our proof combines their reduction with a different argument showing that every nontrivial oriented graph $G$ contains a nonempty set $X$ such that $X^+\ne V(G)$ and $|(X^+)^+\setminus X^+|\geq|X^+\setminus X|$, where $X^+=N_G^+[X]$.

papers.title: Better-than-3 Approximation for 2ECSS Using the Primal-Dual Method
papers.abstract: In the $2$-edge-connected spanning subgraph problem (2ECSS), we are given an undirected multigraph whose edges have nonnegative costs, and the goal is to find a $2$-edge-connected spanning subgraph with minimum total cost. Two distinct approaches yield $2$-approximation algorithms: a reduction to the minimum-cost rooted $2$-arborescence problem and iterative rounding. Despite significant efforts, the best known approximation ratio using the primal-dual method has remained at $3$. Our main result in this work is a primal-dual algorithm for 2ECSS that achieves an approximation ratio of $\sqrt{3}+1 (\leq 2.74)$. The algorithm runs in a single phase and the approximation guarantee is relative to the natural linear relaxation, which requires the sum of the edge variables across every cut to be at least $2$. The algorithm follows the standard template of growing dual variables corresponding to minimal violated sets, albeit at non-uniform rates, until the dual constraint for an edge becomes tight, at which point the edge is temporarily purchased. Once feasibility is attained, redundant edges are dropped in the reverse order in which they were purchased. Our choice of dual growth rates is inspired by the single-phase $3$-approximation algorithm of Beyer, Chimani, and Spoerhase (COCOON 2020). As in their work, our algorithm maintains a forest of purchased edges by repeatedly contracting $2$-edge-connected subgraphs, and dual variables corresponding to leaves and isolated vertices of this forest are grown at a rate of $1$. Our main modification is to additionally grow dual variables corresponding to nontrivial connected components at rate $(\sqrt{3}-1)/2 \approx 0.37$, when the forest is disconnected.

papers.title: Winning and losing NoGo is PSPACE-complete
papers.abstract: We resolve an open problem of Burke and Hearn and show that the combinatorial game NoGo is PSPACE-complete on grids. This is the usual geometry the game is played on, including at the tournament at a 2011 Banff workshop. In addition to this result, we show that it is also PSPACE-complete under mis\`ere play on grids. We prove both of these results using reductions from Bounded Two-Player Constraint Logic. Finally, we show that it is PSPACE-complete under normal play on connected bipartite subcubic graphs.

papers.title: Blow-up size for the noncommutative rank of linear symbolic matrices with low-rank coefficients
papers.abstract: The noncommutative rank (nc-rank) of a linear symbolic matrix $A = A_0 x_0 + A_1 x_1 + \dots + A_m x_m$ is the supremum of $1/k$ times the rank of the $k$-th blow-up $\sum_i A_i \otimes X_i$ of $A$, where $X_i$ are $k \times k$ matrices consisting of distinct variables. In this paper, we show that the blow-up size needed to attain the nc-rank is bounded by the ranks of the coefficient matrices. More precisely, if $A_1, \dots, A_m$ have rank at most $r$, with no restriction on $A_0$, then the $k$-th blow-up attains the nc-rank for every $k \geq r$. This holds for rectangular matrices over an arbitrary field, and unifies and extends the known results that $k = 1$ suffices for rank-one coefficients (Lov\'asz, 1989; Ivanyos, Karpinski, and Saxena, 2010) and that $k = 2$ suffices for skew-symmetric coefficients of rank two (Oki and Soma, 2025). We present two applications. First, if $r$ is a constant, then the nc-rank of an $n \times n$ linear symbolic matrix can be computed by a randomized algorithm with $O(m n^2 + n^\omega)$ arithmetic operations over a sufficiently large field, where $\omega$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. Second, the hierarchy of polytopes introduced by Hirai (2026), which converges to the nc-independent set polytope, stabilizes at the $r$-th level; this is based on a counterpart of our main result for the degree of the Dieudonn\'e determinant.

papers.title: The sharp uniqueness threshold for the antiferromagnetic Potts model on regular trees
papers.abstract: We study Gibbs uniqueness for the $q$-state antiferromagnetic Potts model on the infinite rooted $d$-ary tree and the infinite $(d+1)$-regular tree, where $d\geqslant1$ and $q\geqslant2$. An edge has weight $p\in[0,1]$ if its endpoints have the same color and weight $1$ otherwise. We prove that there is a unique Gibbs state if and only if $p\geqslant p_c:=\max\{0,1-q/(d+1)\}$, except when $(q,p)=(d+1,0)$, thus completes the uniqueness thresholds for all $d\geqslant1$ and $q\geqslant2$. Our proof use a convex potential for the tree recursion and show that it strictly decreases away from the uniform distribution. Together with the result of Gu, Wu and Yang, our theorem gives the exact critical power law whenever $p_c>0$.

papers.title: Schnyder Woods and the Chromatic Polynomial
papers.abstract: Let $\chi_G(q)$ be the chromatic polynomial of a graph $G$. Analogous to the classical results of Greene and Zaslavsky interpreting $(-1)^{n-1}\chi_G'(0)$ and $(-1)^n\chi_G'(1)$ as counting certain orientations of $G$, we show that if $G$ is a triangulation, $\frac{1}{2}(-1)^{n-1}\chi_G'(2)$ counts the number of Schnyder woods on a plane embedding of $G$. We also generalise this result to graphs obtained by removing certain edges of $G$.

papers.title: Elementary first-order model checking for sparse graphs
papers.abstract: It is known that for subgraph-closed graph classes the first-order model checking problem is fixed-parameter tractable if and only if the class is nowhere dense [Grohe, Kreutzer, Siebertz, 2017]. However, the dependency on the formula size is non-elementary, and in fact, this is unavoidable even for the class of all trees [Frick and Grohe, 2004]. On the other hand, it is known that the dependency is elementary for classes of bounded degree [Frick and Grohe, 2004] as well as for classes of bounded pathwidth [Lampis, 2026]. In this paper we generalise these results and almost completely characterise subgraph-closed graph classes for which the model checking problem is fixed-parameter tractable with an elementary dependency on the formula size. Those are the graph classes for which there exists a number $d$ such that for every $r$, some tree of depth $d$ and size bounded by an elementary function of $r$ is avoided as an $(\le r)$-subdivision in all graphs in the class. In particular, this implies that if the class in question excludes a fixed tree as a topological minor, then first-order model checking for graphs in the class is fixed-parameter tractable with an elementary dependency on the formula size.

papers.title: Quickly excluding an apex-forest
papers.abstract: We give a short proof that for every apex-forest $X$ on at least two vertices, graphs excluding $X$ as a minor have layered pathwidth at most $2|V(X)|-3$. This improves upon a result by Dujmovi\'c, Eppstein, Joret, Morin, and Wood (SIDMA, 2020). Our main tool is a structural result about graphs excluding a forest as a rooted minor, which is of independent interest. We develop similar tools for treedepth and treewidth. We discuss implications for Erd\H{o}s-P\'osa properties of rooted models of minors in graphs.

papers.title: Fractional domatic number and minimum degree
papers.abstract: The domatic number of a graph $G$ is the maximum number of pairwise disjoint dominating sets of $G$. We are interested in the LP-relaxation of this parameter, which is called the fractional domatic number of $G$. We study its extremal value in the class of graphs of minimum degree $d$. The fractional domatic number of a graph of minimum degree $d$ is always at most $d+1$, and at least $(1-o(1))\, d/\ln d$ as $d\to \infty$. This is asymptotically tight even within the class of split graphs. Our main result concerns the case $d=2$; we show that, excluding $8$ exceptional graphs, the fractional domatic number of every connected graph of minimum degree (at least) $2$ is at least $5/2$. We also show that this bound cannot be improved if only finitely many graphs are excluded, even for bipartite graphs of arbitrarily large girth. This proves in a stronger sense a conjecture by Gadouleau, Harms, Mertzios, and Zamaraev (2024). This also extends and generalises results from McCuaig and Shepherd (1989), from Fujita, Kameda, and Yamashita (2000), and from Abbas, Egerstedt, Liu, Thomas, and Whalen (2016). Finally, we show that graphs of sub-exponential expansion and sufficiently large girth $g$ have fractional domatic number $3 - o_g(1)$.

papers.title: Log-concavity and Approximate Counting for Totally Unimodular Polytopes
papers.abstract: We present a new lower bound on the number of lattice points of all totally unimodular polytopes, generalizing previous lower bounds on contingency tables, integer flows, and beyond. Our bound is based on the Gurvits capacity convex optimization problem, and thus our result implies an efficient deterministic algorithm for approximate counting of the lattice points up to an explicit exponential factor. We achieve our bounds by showing that the associated generating polynomials fit into a new general class of log-concave polynomials called VLC ("variable-wise log-concavity''). This also implies a conjecture of Ferroni and Higashitani on the evaluations of the Ehrhart polynomials of unimodular polytopes. The essential ingredient for these results is the resolution of Barvinok's log-concavity conjecture for contingency tables on lines, which was proven using ChatGPT 6 Astra. We conjecture a generalization of Barvinok's conjecture, which we believe will lead to stronger and more general bounds.

papers.title: How many sorted projections determine any n points in k dimensions?
papers.abstract: Let $d_1,\dots,d_m$ be directions in $\mathbb{R}^k$, where $k\ge 2$. A multiset $X$ of $n$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ projects to the $m$ multisets of numbers $\{\{x\cdot d_j : x\in X\}\}$, or equivalently to the $m$ sorted lists of these numbers. How many directions are needed for these projections to determine every multiset of $n$ points? Two simple bounds are known in every dimension: more than $(k-1)\log_2 n$ directions are always needed, and $(k-1)n+1$ directions in general position always suffice. In the plane much more is known: Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron showed that almost every choice of $O(\log n \log\log n)$ directions suffices. Whether anything similar holds in higher dimensions was left open by Dym, Wellershoff, Tsoukanis, Levy and Balan. We observe that two lemmas of Hair and Sahai, proved for list recovery of random linear codes, answer that question, and by tightening their argument we show that in every dimension almost every choice of $(4k-2)\ln(2n)\ln(k\log_2 2n)+k+1$ directions suffices. For $k\le 10$ this beats the linear bound once $n$ is larger than about 100: for example, 144 directions suffice for multisets of 1000 points in the plane, and an exact computation lowers this to 133. Letting some of the random blocks in their argument fail removes a factor $\log k$: almost every choice of $O(k\log n\log\log n)$ directions suffices, uniformly in $k$ and $n$. We also show that $2k-1$ directions never determine three points, so that the logarithmic lower bound is not tight; that every $m$ directions in the plane fail on some pair of multisets of size $O(1.65^m)$, improving the bound $O(1.80^m)$ of Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron; and that for each $k$, $m$ and $n$, either almost every choice of $m$ directions works or almost none does.

papers.title: A Proof of Blackburn's Conjecture on Non-Overlapping Codes
papers.abstract: A code is non-overlapping if no nonempty proper prefix of a codeword is a suffix of a codeword. Let $S_n(q)$ be the largest size of a non-overlapping code of length $n$ over an alphabet of size $q$. Levenshtein proved that $S_n(q)\le c_nq^n$, where $c_n=(1/n)\bigl((n-1)/n\bigr)^{n-1}$. The codes $I^{n-1}J$, where $I$ and $J$ partition the alphabet, attain this bound when $n$ divides $q$, and Blackburn conjectured that for every $n$ and all sufficiently large $q$, the best such code is a maximum non-overlapping code. We prove this conjecture. The proof uses generating functions for the nested partitions that describe maximal non-overlapping codes. We also show that only the codes $I^{n-1}J$ with $|I|=(n-1)q/n$ and their reversals meet Levenshtein's bound.

papers.title: Path Cover, Hamiltonicity, and Independence Number: An FPT Perspective
papers.abstract: The classic theorem of Gallai and Milgram (1960) asserts that for every graph \(G\), the vertex set of \(G\) can be partitioned into at most \(\alpha(G)\) vertex-disjoint paths, where \(\alpha(G)\) is the maximum size of an independent set in \(G\). While the Gallai-Milgram theorem is tight, it was not known prior to our work whether deciding if a graph \(G\) could be covered by fewer than \(\alpha(G)\) vertex-disjoint paths can be done in polynomial time. We resolve this question by proving the following algorithmic extension of the Gallai-Milgram theorem for undirected graphs: There is an algorithm that, for an \(n\)-vertex graph \(G\) and an integer parameter \(k \ge 1\), runs in time \(2^{2^{\Oh(k^4\log{k})}} \cdot n^{\Oh(1)}\) and outputs a path cover \(\mathcal{P}\) of \(G\) together with either a correct conclusion that \(\mathcal{P}\) is a minimum-size path cover, or an independent set of size \(\lvert \mathcal{P}\rvert + k\), certifying that \(\mathcal{P}\) contains at most \(\alpha(G) - k\) paths. One of the key subroutines in our algorithm is a fixed-parameter tractable FPT algorithm, parameterized by \(\alpha(G)\), for deciding whether \(G\) contains a Hamiltonian path. This result is of independent interest---prior to our work, no polynomial-time algorithm for deciding Hamiltonicity was known even for graphs with independence number at most three. Moreover, the algorithmic techniques we develop apply to a wide array of problems in undirected graphs, including Hamiltonian Cycle, Path Cover, Largest Linkage, and Topological Minor Containment. We show that all these problems are FPT when parameterized by the independence number of the graph.
